name: WebGL renderer and parameters
plain: Reads the graphics card name and GPU capability values.
meaning: Reveals the GPU vendor and model and a set of limits, which together identify a hardware class and often a precise device.

limits.headline: Can see your graphics card name and its capability limits
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when the page loads
can: Get your graphics card maker and model
Get a set of hardware limits
Often narrow you to a small group of devices
cannot: Get the exact model in browsers that hide or round it, such as Safari or Brave
limits.differs: Chrome and Edge show the graphics card model. Safari and Brave hide or generalise it.

story.what_it_is: A page reads your graphics card's name and its capability values, usually without any prompt.

marketing.name: WebGL API
marketing.pitch: Lets a page draw 2D and 3D graphics in the browser using the graphics chip, with no plugin.

marketing.name: WebGL
marketing.pitch: The group behind the standard describes it as hardware accelerated 3D graphics for the web.

story.for_you: You see games, maps and 3D tools that run smoothly in the tab. You are never asked, and the page can see which graphics chip you have and what it can do.
story.for_makers: Browser games, 3D product viewers and design tools use your graphics card to look good. They read the graphics name and limits to pick the right quality. Trackers read the same values for device IDs.

use_cases.example: Krunker.io and Shell Shockers run full 3D shooters in a tab using WebGL, and set quality by your graphics chip.
Google Earth and Mapbox draw the 3D globe, buildings and terrain on your graphics card.
Figma draws huge design files using WebGL so zooming and panning stays smooth.
A 3D shoe or furniture viewer lets you spin a product, using your graphics chip.
A tracker reads the graphics card name and adds it to a device ID.
A fraud engine sees a graphics name from a cloud server and treats the visit as a bot risk.
A science site shows a 3D model of a cell or planet you can rotate with your mouse.

technical_bounds: Firefox and Safari may mask the renderer
